stem.text: The manganate(VII) ion, MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup>, is used in chemistry as an oxidising agent.
Three reactions each involve MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> as a reagent.
reaction 2: MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> + 5Fe<sup>2+</sup> + 8H<sup>+</sup> → Mn<sup>2+</sup> + 5Fe<sup>3+</sup> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O
reaction 3: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> + 3[O] → C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O
reaction 4: MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> + 4Mn(OH)<sub>2</sub> + 16H<sup>+</sup> → 5Mn<sup>3+</sup> + 12H<sub>2</sub>O
Oxygen slowly oxidises Fe<sup>2+</sup>(aq). Reaction 2 can be used to determine the percentage of Fe<sup>2+</sup>(aq) that is oxidised over a certain time.

A student prepares a 250 cm<sup>3</sup> solution using 17.70 g of FeSO<sub>4</sub>•7H<sub>2</sub>O. After one week, the student titrates 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> portions of this solution with acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>(aq) of concentration 0.0500 mol dm<sup>–3</sup>.
The average titre is 23.80 cm<sup>3</sup>.
Calculate the percentage of Fe<sup>2+</sup> ions in the original sample that were oxidised during one week.
[M<sub>r</sub>: FeSO<sub>4</sub>•7H<sub>2</sub>O, 277.9]

points.text: M1: moles of manganate = 23.80/1000 × 0.0500 OR 1.19×10<sup>–3</sup> mol
alternatives: initial moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> = 17.70 ÷ 277.9 OR 6.37×10<sup>–2</sup> mol

points.text: M2: moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> in aliquot = 5 × 1.19×10<sup>–3</sup> OR 5.95×10<sup>–3</sup> mol AND total moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> = 5.95×10<sup>–3</sup> × 10 OR 5.95×10<sup>–2</sup> mol
alternatives: mass of FeSO<sub>4</sub>·7H<sub>2</sub>O left = 5.95×10<sup>–3</sup> × 277.9 OR 1.6535 g (in 25 cm<sup>3</sup>)

points.text: M3: mass of FeSO<sub>4</sub>·7H<sub>2</sub>O left = 1.6535 g × 10 = 16.535 g (in 250 cm<sup>3</sup>)

markScheme.note: MS labels steps M1/M2/M3 plus a final 'percentage oxidised' line; n=1-4 kept sequential for ref purposes.

explanation.text: This is a redox titration back-calculation. First use the titre to find moles of MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> used (0.02380 dm<sup>3</sup> × 0.0500 mol dm<sup>–3</sup>), then reaction 2's 1:5 ratio (MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup>:Fe<sup>2+</sup>) to find moles of Fe<sup>2+</sup> remaining in that 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> aliquot, then scale up ×10 to the full 250 cm<sup>3</sup>, then convert moles of remaining Fe<sup>2+</sup> back into a mass of FeSO<sub>4</sub>·7H<sub>2</sub>O (using M<sub>r</sub> = 277.9) to compare directly with the 17.70 g originally weighed out. The mass lost (oxidised away) divided by the original mass, ×100%, gives the percentage oxidised.

reasoningChain: Moles MnO4⁻ titrated = concentration × titre volume.
Scale by the 1:5 mole ratio in reaction 2 to get moles Fe²⁺ remaining in the 25.0 cm³ aliquot.
Multiply by 10 to get total moles (then mass) of Fe²⁺ remaining in the full 250 cm³.
Compare that remaining mass with the original 17.70 g to find the mass (and hence %) oxidised away.

inferredMistakes.text: Calculating the mass of FeSO4·7H2O remaining correctly but then dividing that remaining mass by the original mass (giving 93.4%, the percentage NOT oxidised) instead of subtracting first, as the ER reports.
Omitting the ×10 scale-up from the 25.0 cm³ aliquot to the full 250 cm³ solution, giving 90.7%, as the ER reports.

stem.text: Explain why an indicator is not needed in this titration.

alternatives: solution changes (from colourless) to pink/purple at the end-point

explanation.text: KMnO<sub>4</sub> is intensely coloured (deep purple) while its reduction product Mn<sup>2+</sup>(aq) is almost colourless, so MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> acts as its own ('self') indicator: the solution stays colourless while MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> is being used up, and the end-point is seen as the first permanent trace of pink/purple colour once no more Fe<sup>2+</sup> remains to react with the next drop.

reasoningChain: Note MnO4⁻ is strongly coloured and Mn²⁺ is not.
Conclude the colour change of the reagent itself marks the end-point, so no separate indicator is needed.

inferredMistakes.text: Describing the colour change the wrong way round (from colourless to purple) rather than purple/pink appearing at the end-point, which the ER reports as a common imprecision.

stem.text: Reaction 3 uses hot alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub> as the reagent. The reaction mixture is then acidified.
Draw the structure of the organic product, C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, of reaction 3.

points.text: benzene ring with a side-chain –COOH group (benzoic acid)

markScheme.note: The MS answer is a drawn structure (benzoic acid); shown as ms.figure.

figure.alt: Structural formula of benzoic acid: a benzene ring with a side-chain -COOH group.

explanation.text: Hot alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub> is a strong oxidising agent that oxidises the methyl side-chain of methylbenzene (toluene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) all the way to a carboxylic acid group, giving benzoic acid, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH (molecular formula C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, matching the question). The ring itself is not attacked under these conditions.

reasoningChain: Recognise C7H6O2 as benzoic acid's molecular formula.
Draw the benzene ring with a side-chain COOH group in place of the original CH3 group.

stem.text: Reaction 4 is called a reverse disproportionation reaction.
Suggest the meaning of reverse disproportionation. Use oxidation numbers to explain your reasoning.

points.text: manganese is both oxidised and reduced (to a single oxidation state)

points.note: AND is in bold in the MS: both oxidation-number changes are required for this point.

explanation.text: Disproportionation is a single element being simultaneously oxidised and reduced in the same reaction, starting from one oxidation state and splitting into two different ones. 'Reverse' disproportionation is the opposite: manganese starts the reaction in two different oxidation states (MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> has Mn at +VII, and Mn(OH)<sub>2</sub> has Mn at +II) and both end up at a single, common oxidation state (Mn<sup>3+</sup>, +III). The +VII Mn is reduced (gains electrons, oxidation number falls to +III) while the +II Mn is oxidised (loses electrons, oxidation number rises to +III) — one species reduced, the other oxidised, converging on the same product.

reasoningChain: Identify the two starting oxidation states of Mn: +7 (in MnO4⁻) and +2 (in Mn(OH)2).
Identify the single final oxidation state: +3 (in Mn3+).
State that the +7 species is reduced and the +2 species is oxidised, both converging on +3 — the reverse of normal disproportionation.

inferredMistakes.text: Explaining the reaction using the formulas/charges of the ions (e.g. 'Mn7+ and Mn2+ forming Mn3+') instead of oxidation numbers, which the ER reports as insufficient since the question explicitly asks for oxidation numbers.

stem.text: The solubility of Mn(OH)<sub>2</sub> in water is 3.20 × 10<sup>–3</sup> g dm<sup>–3</sup> at 298 K.
Write an expression for the solubility product, K<sub>sp</sub>, of Mn(OH)<sub>2</sub>.

explanation.text: Mn(OH)<sub>2</sub> dissociates as Mn(OH)<sub>2</sub>(s) ⇌ Mn<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + 2OH<sup>–</sup>(aq). The solubility product expression is the product of the ionic concentrations, each raised to the power of its stoichiometric coefficient in the dissociation: [Mn<sup>2+</sup>] from the single Mn<sup>2+</sup> ion, [OH<sup>–</sup>]<sup>2</sup> because two OH<sup>–</sup> ions are produced per formula unit.

reasoningChain: Write the dissociation equation for Mn(OH)2.
Write Ksp as the product of ion concentrations raised to their stoichiometric powers.

inferredMistakes.text: Omitting the charges on the ions in the Ksp expression (writing [Mn][OH]² rather than [Mn2+][OH–]²), which the ER reports as a common slip.

stem.text: Calculate the value of K<sub>sp</sub> of Mn(OH)<sub>2</sub> at 298 K. State its units.

explanation.text: First convert the given solubility from g dm<sup>–3</sup> to mol dm<sup>–3</sup> using M<sub>r</sub>(Mn(OH)<sub>2</sub>) = 88.9: 3.20×10<sup>–3</sup>/88.9 = 3.60×10<sup>–5</sup> mol dm<sup>–3</sup>. This is [Mn<sup>2+</sup>], since each formula unit that dissolves gives one Mn<sup>2+</sup>. [OH<sup>–</sup>] is twice this (2 × 3.60×10<sup>–5</sup>), since two OH<sup>–</sup> are released per formula unit. Substitute into K<sub>sp</sub> = [Mn<sup>2+</sup>][OH<sup>–</sup>]<sup>2</sup> = 3.60×10<sup>–5</sup> × (7.20×10<sup>–5</sup>)<sup>2</sup>, which simplifies to 4 × (3.60×10<sup>–5</sup>)<sup>3</sup> = 1.87×10<sup>–13</sup>. Units come from the expression itself: mol dm<sup>–3</sup> × (mol dm<sup>–3</sup>)<sup>2</sup> = mol<sup>3</sup> dm<sup>–9</sup>.

reasoningChain: Convert the given solubility (g dm⁻³) to mol dm⁻³ using the molar mass of Mn(OH)2 — this equals [Mn²⁺].
Double it to get [OH⁻] (2 mol OH⁻ per mol Mn(OH)2 dissolved).
Substitute both into the Ksp expression from d(i) and calculate.
Derive the units directly from the expression: (mol dm⁻³)×(mol dm⁻³)² = mol³ dm⁻⁹.

inferredMistakes.text: Not converting the given solubility from g dm⁻³ to mol dm⁻³ before substituting into the Ksp expression, which the ER reports as a common error (leading to an error-carried-forward value of 1.31×10⁻⁷).

stem.text: Mn<sup>3+</sup>(aq) ions are coloured. Explain why.

points.text: d orbital(s) of two different energies/d-d splitting occurs

alternatives: radiation/energy from visible (region) absorbed AND colour (seen) is complementary

explanation.text: In the free (isolated) Mn<sup>3+</sup> ion, the five d orbitals are all the same energy (degenerate). When ligands (e.g. water) bond to the ion, their electric field splits the d orbitals into two sets of different energy (d-d splitting). An electron can be promoted/excited from the lower-energy set to the higher-energy set by absorbing a photon of exactly the right energy (matching the gap, ΔE = hf). Since Mn<sup>3+</sup> has d electrons available to promote, this absorption happens in the visible region; the colour seen is the complementary colour to the light absorbed (the wavelengths not absorbed are transmitted/reflected to the eye).

reasoningChain: State that ligands cause the d orbitals to split into two energy levels.
State that an electron is promoted/excited from the lower to the higher level.
State that this promotion absorbs a specific wavelength/frequency of visible light, and the complementary colour is seen/transmitted.

inferredMistakes.text: Describing light being emitted rather than absorbed by the d-d transition, which the ER reports as a common error — colour in transition metal ions comes from selective absorption, not emission.

stem.text: Mn<sup>3+</sup> ions form the complex ion [Mn(C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>3–</sup>, which shows stereoisomerism.

Complete Table 2.1 to give details of this complex. Use a curved bracket linking two O atoms to represent the ligands in the three-dimensional structures of the stereoisomers of [Mn(C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>3–</sup>.

type of stereoisomerism shown by complex

stem.note: QP prints this as a mostly-blank table for the candidate to complete; only the top row (formula of complex) and the 'optical' row are pre-filled.

points.text: structures: two mirror-image three-dimensional structures of [Mn(C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>]<sup>3–</sup>, each Mn bonded to three bidentate C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup> ligands arranged octahedrally, correct wedge/dash 3-D bond notation and square-bracket/charge notation

markScheme.note: See figures/q2_ms_stereoisomers.png for the MS's two printed optical-isomer structures (point 4).

figure.alt: The two mirror-image three-dimensional structures of the octahedral complex ion.

explanation.text: The oxalate ion, C<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub><sup>2–</sup>, is bidentate: it donates two lone pairs (one from each of two O atoms) to the metal, so three oxalate ligands occupy all 6 coordination positions around Mn<sup>3+</sup>, giving coordination number 6 and an octahedral shape. Because the complex has no plane of symmetry when all three bidentate ligands are arranged this way, it is chiral: the two non-superimposable mirror-image arrangements are the optical isomers shown in the MS, drawn with correct 3-D wedge/dash bonds and each oxalate ligand shown as a curved line joining its two donating O atoms.

reasoningChain: Identify C2O4²⁻ (oxalate) as a bidentate ligand donating 2 lone pairs each.
Three bidentate ligands × 2 donor atoms = coordination number 6, giving an octahedral shape.
Draw the two non-superimposable mirror-image 3-D structures (optical isomers) using correct wedge/dash notation and curved lines for each ligand.

inferredMistakes.text: Giving the ligand formula without its 2– charge (e.g. C2O4 instead of C2O42–), which the ER reports as a common omission.
Drawing the three-dimensional structures with an incorrect orientation of the wedge/dash bonds, which the ER explicitly flags as a common error and illustrates the expected orientation.
